title: Episodes and Semantics: Their Overlap, Cooperation, and Distinctions

Recent research increasingly suggests that episodic and semantic memory are not separate, isolated systems, but rather points along a continuum of declarative memory that engage a common core network to different degrees. Neural evidence shows a substantial overlap in the brain regions involved in both episodic and semantic retrieval. All types of long-term memory - from impersonal facts to personal facts to rich recollections - activate a shared "core memory network" including the medial temporal lobes (hippocampus and associated structures), medial prefrontal cortex, and posterior parietal cortex. The distinction between simulating an event versus knowing a fact appears to arise from quantitative differences in the magnitude and pattern of activation within this common network, rather than entirely different circuits. For example, retrieving a unique, vivid event (classic episodic memory) elicits a stronger ramp-up of activity in hippocampal, posterior parietal, and medial prefrontal regions compared to recalling a general piece of knowledge, with intermediate levels of engagement for "in-between" cases like memories of a repeated routine. This continuum perspective calls into question the once-standard view of completely distinct systems, instead indicating that the distinction between semantic and episodic inference is more or less a distinction resulting from the activity of similar components across time: the 5D (3D space, 1D time, and 1D activity) activity profile of the system’s components determines the location of the psychological product on the semantic-episodic continuum. The schema–novelty framework distinguishes updating an old model from creating a new one (Figure) 10. The narrative task separates schema structure from individual stories (Figure) 11.

In operational terms, the system defaults to semantic retrieval when the cue sits in a dense, well-learned region of conceptual space and/or the cost of latency is high: vmPFC and anterior temporal hubs return a compressed prototype or rule that is ’good enough’ without reinstating context. It recruits episodic simulation when expected gains from reinstating spatiotemporal structure outweigh the costs-when cues are novel or ambiguous, when the query requires WWW binding or counterfactual recombination, or when the transition model may have changed. Formally, arbitration follows an expected-value-of-computation policy in which semantic memory provides fast, low-variance estimates and episodic memory provides slower, high-fidelity samples that reduce uncertainty or expose edge-cases. Strong schemas push the balance toward semantic reuse and rapid integration; weak or violated schemas shift weight to hippocampal construction. This rule explains everyday behavior: you answer ’What’s the capital of France?’ semantically; you answer ’Would I enjoy a sauna after heavy deadlifts?’ by simulating specific episodes; you choose a restaurant in your home city semantically (scripts, prototypes), but in a new country by sampling episodes, reading off WWW details, and updating the semantic map.

One key hub in the unified memory network is the hippocampus. Long known for its role in episodic recollection, the hippocampus is now understood to be deeply involved in semantic memory as well. It is critical for encoding new semantic information and can be recruited during semantic retrieval, especially when relationships or context must be processed 1. In fact, recent reviews reaffirm that both episodic and semantic memories are relational and (re)constructive, relying on the hippocampal formation to bind together elements into coherent representations. The rich associations that give semantic knowledge its structure (e.g. how concepts link to one another) and give episodic events their situational detail (who, what, where, when) both depend on hippocampal-dependent coding of relationships. Damage to the hippocampus tends to impair not only the ability to re-experience past events, but also the acquisition of new factual knowledge - underscoring that hippocampal computations support both kinds of memory content. Still, there are differences in degree: during a truly episodic memory task (say, recalling a specific birthday party), hippocampal and related "internal mentation" regions often show greater activity than during a purely semantic task (e.g. recalling what the capital of France is). Recent sequence-learning work shows the hippocampus integrating related events into representations that support novel multistep prediction (Figure) 9. At a representational level, mounting evidence suggests that both episodic and semantic memories are organized in brain networks as cognitive maps or graphs, and that retrieving a memory involves a process akin to navigation. The hippocampo-entorhinal system famously supports spatial navigation, and an emerging view is that this system also encodes abstract relationships among experiences and concepts in a map-like format 2. In other words, neurons that map physical space (place cells, grid cells, etc.) may similarly map conceptual "spaces," allowing us to mentally wander through knowledge just as we would wander through a landscape. This idea is consistent with the aforementioned studies of human semantic retrieval, where people are shown to "forage" through semantic space: remembering episodes and retrieving facts might leverage a common spatial-navigation-derived mechanism - effectively moving along paths in an internal cognitive map 3. Episodic recollection can be seen as a journey through the time and place of a past event, and semantic recall as a journey through a network of related concepts. In both cases, the trajectory our mind takes (traversing associative links or spatial-temporal context) reflects a shared computational heritage. A 2026 predictive-mapping study models subicular spatial responses (Figure) 14.

Despite these deep commonalities, there are clear qualitative distinctions between an episodic memory and a semantic memory in terms of phenomenological detail and format. Episodic memories are often described as being "re-experienced" rather than just known. They contain richly bound What-Where-When (WWW) elements - the specific persons, objects, places, and the temporal sequence of events - all embedded into a single mental reconstruction 4, 5. Such memories have an internal spatiotemporal structure: one can say that in an episodic recall, you know not just what happened, but where each element was relative to others ("next to") and when things occurred ("before/after" something else), and you often recall the event from a particular perspective (usually your own) with accompanying sensory details and emotions. In other words, episodic recall attempts to reinstate the multidimensional context of an experience - yielding a "holistic" representation with the feel of mentally traveling back in time. By contrast, semantic memory stores more decontextualized knowledge. A semantic memory might be the fact "saunas are hot, steamy, and relaxing", divorced from any particular time or personal experience. An episodic memory, on the other hand, would be "I remember the Friday night when I won a dare to stay the longest in a sauna - it was so hot and we celebrated afterward with cucumber water". The latter is singular, tied to a specific when and where, and laden with perceptual detail (the heat, the taste of the water), whereas the former is a general truth accumulated from many instances. Indeed, neuropsychology has long noted that patients can lose the ability to vividly re-live events (episodic impairment) while still knowing facts, and vice versa, highlighting that the presence of contextual detail is a key differentiator. Modern views, however, stress this is a difference in degree and kind of information represented, not a wholly separate memory store - episodic memory simply sits at the extreme end of high-detail, high-context "episodicness," whereas semantic memory lies at the other end of low-context, generalized knowledge. The behavioral comparison separates generalization from detailed recognition (Figure) 13.

Crucially, episodic and semantic memory cooperate during both learning and retrieval, each supporting the other. During learning, episodic experiences are a primary source of new semantic knowledge. Recalling or replaying specific episodes can lead to the extraction of general principles or facts - a process sometimes dubbed "semanticization." For example, a person who vividly remembers a series of individual chemistry experiments (episodic) may over time abstract from them the general scientific concepts or rules (semantic). In cognitive neuroscience, this idea is captured by consolidation theories: initially, new information is encoded episodically with hippocampal involvement; with repeated reactivation of the memory (e.g. recalling or reflecting on the event), the hippocampal-cortical network gradually distills the common elements and stores them in the cortex as semantic knowledge. Empirical evidence supports this gradual gist abstraction: repeatedly recalling a past event tends to reinforce the central ideas while certain contextual details fade, resulting in a more schematic version of the memory. For instance, over months or years you might forget exactly which day a particular meeting took place (episodic detail) but remember the outcome or knowledge gained from it (now part of your semantic memory). In neurological patients, we see the other side of this coin: damage that prevents forming new episodic memories (e.g. hippocampal amnesia) also severely impairs the learning of new facts, unless alternative pathways are leveraged. Likewise, there is often a gradual transformation of memories from episodic to semantic form. Initially, a memory of a learning event is rich in context, but with time and repeated exposure, it becomes "known" independent of the original context. This can happen slowly or, if the new information fits an existing schema, quite rapidly. Research indicates that when new information is schema-consistent (fits prior knowledge), the brain can integrate it into semantic memory very quickly - sometimes bypassing the need for prolonged hippocampal replay. On the other hand, schema-inconsistent information (truly novel structures) usually requires more hippocampal engagement and consolidation time to become integrated. Thus, episodic memory provides a training ground or "gateway" for semantic learning, and having a rich base of semantic schemas in turn can accelerate new episodic experiences being generalized. The representational comparison distinguishes shared schema from episode-specific content (Figure). The memory results illustrate how prior knowledge changes acquisition (Figure) 12.

During retrieval and inference, the two forms of memory are likewise interwoven. Remembering a specific episode often requires semantic support to fill in gaps and guide the search. Our semantic knowledge about the world provides context that helps us reconstruct events: for example, knowing typical scripts or schemas ("what usually happens at a birthday party") will guide and scaffold the retrieval of a particular birthday party memory. If semantic memory is compromised, episodic recollection suffers. In semantic dementia (a neurodegenerative disease that erodes semantic knowledge), patients can often recall recent experiences to some extent, but their ability to retrieve older, more remote autobiographical episodes degrades in tandem with their loss of general knowledge 5. They might remember isolated sensory fragments of an event but struggle to place them in a coherent narrative, effectively "falling back" on over-general memories of the sort "something usually happens" without specifics. This happens because without the semantic framework (e.g. understanding who people are, what typical contexts mean, the narrative structure of events), the hippocampal pattern completion has little scaffold on which to hang the retrieved perceptual details. Conversely, semantic memory retrieval can be enriched or supported by episodic simulation. We often answer ostensibly semantic questions by mentally simulating episodes. For instance, to answer a question like "Do I like saunas?", one might remember a particular sauna visit (an episode) and derive the answer from it (concluding "Yes, because in that episode I felt great"). In this way, episodic memory can produce on-the-fly "semantic" information - effectively extracting general knowledge from a specific reconstruction. Researchers have termed such on-demand abstraction as episodic memory enabling "prototypically semantic" inferences 6. Even when we think we are using pure semantic memory, subtle experiments show that we often tap into episodic traces (especially for personal or experiential knowledge) to inform our judgments. Neuroimaging reveals that tasks requiring flexible inference or novel combination of knowledge (like figuring out a puzzle) activate episodic retrieval networks alongside semantic areas, indicating the brain recruits episodic simulation to supplement semantic reasoning. A virtual-reality task tests how new links integrate previously separate event sequences (Figure). Hippocampal sequence integration predicts improved multistep behavioral predictions (Figure).

Personal semantic memory occupies a middle ground in this interplay. Personal semantics refers to one’s store of factual knowledge about their own life - e.g. "I have a gym membership" or "I used to go jogging every Sunday." These are facts (thus semantic-like) but also personal and derived from repeated episodes (thus episodic-like). Conceptually, personal semantic memory lies between general semantic and fully episodic memory. Its neural correlates reflect this: for example, remembering an autobiographical fact (like your first phone number) engages the core memory network less than recalling a unique event, but often more than impersonal facts 7. Some personal semantics (especially repeated-event memories, like "my Sunday jogging routine") recruit brain activity very similar to recalling a generic episode, whereas other personal facts (like your own street address) behave more like pure semantics in the brain. Functionally, personal semantic knowledge can serve as a powerful retrieval cue for episodic memory. Knowing the general schema of your life - e.g. that "I usually do stretches before a workout" - can help trigger a memory of a specific instance ("that time last week at the gym when I stretched and then tried a new exercise") by providing a scaffold to search within. Studies indeed suggest that having rich personal semantics (like well-developed life schemas or narratives) is associated with better access to detailed autobiographical episodes. Moreover, personal semantic memories themselves often originate through the repeated replay of episodic events until they lose their context - a process sometimes observed during memory consolidation when frequent experiences (like going to the gym every week) blur into a generalized memory of one’s habits.

The tight coupling between semantic scaffolds and episodic details becomes especially apparent in prospective memory - imagining or planning for the future. Episodic future thinking (EFT), the ability to construct plausible future scenarios, draws on both systems. To imagine a novel event (say, a future vacation), one must flexibly recombine bits of past episodic memories (sights, sounds, places one has been) and incorporate semantic knowledge about the world (what typically happens on vacations, what one knows about the destination, etc.). Semantic memory provides the semantic and schematic context that keeps an imagined scenario coherent. Individuals with semantic memory loss dramatically illustrate this: patients with semantic dementia can often describe past events they lived through, but when asked to imagine a new event, they struggle greatly. Lacking general knowledge of people, objects, and schemas, their attempts at future simulation often degrade into disjointed "replays" of actual past events or a collection of unconnected fragments; one study found that  80% of the "future" events described by semantic dementia patients were essentially replays of previously experienced events 5. This phenomenon supports the semantic scaffolding hypothesis, which posits that conceptual semantic knowledge provides a necessary framework for building both richly detailed memories and novel imagined scenarios 5. Without that scaffold, episodic details - no matter how vivid - cannot be bound into a coherent, chronological narrative. On the flip side, when the episodic system is compromised (as in some cases of amnesia), people can still often imagine general future events in semantic terms (e.g. "I will probably eat dinner, because I know I usually do"), but they cannot envision them with the specificity of a real episode. Thus, both past- and future-oriented mental time travel rely on an interplay: episodic memory supplies the experiential building blocks, while semantic memory ensures those blocks fit into a sensible structure. In sum, episodic and semantic memory are deeply interdependent, each providing material and constraints for the other: episodic recollection lets us relive and recombine raw experience, but semantic frameworks knit those experiences into organized knowledge and plausible imaginings.

One compelling application of this episodic-semantic synergy is in creative thinking. Creativity - generating ideas that are both novel and useful - turns out to be a memory-intensive process, drawing on our stores of knowledge and experiences and recombining them in new ways. A recent framework called MemiC ("Memory in Creative Ideation") 8 makes the episodic-semantic continuum operational for creativity by carving ideation into four interactive stages - search, construction, novelty evaluation, and effectiveness evaluation - and by specifying how controlled and associative processes recruit semantic and episodic memory at each step.

In the search stage, semantic memory is the workhorse for rapid, breadth-first access to concepts - broad retrieval ability strongly predicts the fluency and originality of ideas - but episodic memory adds crucial, high-variance samples that widen the search frontier. Brief "episodic specificity" inductions that train people to unpack concrete event details boost idea fluency on divergent thinking tasks, and when hippocampal-DMN nodes are perturbed with TMS or direct cortical stimulation, fluent idea production drops, indicating a causal contribution of episodic retrieval to candidate generation. Practically, people mix strategies: they query semantic neighborhoods (category/property cues, remote associates) while also "walking around" remembered scenes to harvest candidates (for example, mentally touring a zoo during animal fluency). The upshot is cooperative: semantic search raises recall probability for many relevant items; episodic search injects distinctive, recombinable particulars.

Construction turns what search finds into candidate solutions via two partially dissociable mechanisms that nonetheless share substrates. On the semantic side, construction forges new links among weakly related concepts (remote associations, multiply-constrained search), and people higher in creative ability are better at generating such bi-associations. On the episodic side, construction runs mental simulations that recombine multimodal fragments into plausible scenes or object manipulations. Neurocognitively, construction draws on hippocampus-anchored default-mode circuitry while engaging control regions to keep the recombination goal-directed; the same system that supports episodic simulation also ramps during the creation of novel semantic links, underscoring the shared, relational machinery behind both "knowing" and "imagining."

Novelty evaluation then compares the constructed candidate against what is already known or experienced. Here, semantic knowledge provides a fast familiarity metric (is this association in the graph?), while episodic memory checks it against lived instances. Imaging work isolates a left supramarginal gyrus signal that tracks novelty judgments over and above usefulness, suggesting a dedicated comparator that feeds back to generation when an idea looks familiar. Functionally, novelty checks prune obvious, overlearned outputs and push search toward remoter regions of both the semantic network and the episodic archive.

Effectiveness evaluation is a different beast: instead of "have I seen/thought this before?" the question is "would this actually work?". Semantic memory supplies prototypes, affordances, and constraints that let you quickly reject infeasible constructions; episodic memory supplies the simulator to run mental feasibility tests under context and dynamics. Across tasks, effectiveness judgments elicit stronger engagement of hippocampus, angular gyrus, and posterior cingulate - the same episodic-simulation network - and, tellingly, effective ideas drive more activation than ineffective ones, consistent with simulation-based "stress testing" of the candidate. This stage is where the systems are most complementary: semantics frames the evaluation criteria; episodes supply counterfactual rollouts that expose hidden failure modes or reveal a path to implementation.

Looping these stages yields the practical algorithm of creative cognition: controlled cues bias memory search; semantic and episodic construction synthesize candidates; novelty vetoes the cliché; effectiveness vetting, powered by episodic simulation but guided by semantic constraints, selects for useful originality. MemiC’s contribution is to show that this is not a hand-off between two separate stores but a coordination of shared, relational machinery tuned across tasks and timescales - exactly what a continuum view predicts.

In closing, the interplay between episodic and semantic memory is best understood not as a meeting of two isolated faculties, but as a dynamic, bidirectional exchange within a shared relational architecture. They trade in different currencies-episodic memory in richly contextualized reconstructions of specific experiences, semantic memory in abstracted, generalized knowledge-but each continually seeds, constrains, and reshapes the other. This mutual scaffolding is evident in learning, retrieval, imagination, and creative ideation: episodes provide the raw, detail-rich building blocks that keep knowledge grounded in lived reality, while semantic structures offer the organizing principles, schemas, and inferential shortcuts that keep recollection and invention coherent. This synergy enables not only accurate remembering and efficient knowledge use, but also the recombinative leaps that underpin planning, problem-solving, and creative thought.
